analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to list PFAS chemicals as toxic pollutants and set clean water discharge limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or floor vote, dying at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are long-lasting man-made chemicals used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, food packaging, and firefighting foam, and they may harm human health [S2]. The bill would have required the EPA, within 30 days of enactment, to add PFAS to the official list of toxic pollutants under the Clean Water Act, and required the EPA to set discharge limits for factories and pretreatment requirements for industrial users of sewage treatment plants by January 1, 2022 [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water or eat fish affected by PFAS discharges, and communities near industrial facilities that release these chemicals into rivers and streams. Setting enforceable effluent and pretreatment standards would cap how much PFAS factories and sewage systems can release into waterways [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities exposed to PFAS water contamination

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to add PFAS to the Clean Water Act's list of toxic pollutants within 30 days of enactment, without waiting for the usual agency factor-by-factor evaluation [S3].
Directs the EPA to publish effluent standards for PFAS by January 1, 2022, legally limiting how much of these chemicals industrial facilities may discharge into waterways [S3].
Requires pretreatment standards under Clean Water Act section 307(b) by the same deadline, so PFAS entering sewage treatment plants from industrial users is controlled at the source [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and industrial facilities that discharge PFAS into water — including makers of nonstick products, waterproof textiles, and paper and metal-plating operations — would bear the cost of meeting new discharge limits and pretreatment requirements, some of which may be passed to consumers in product prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a fixed 30-day deadline to add all PFAS to the toxic pollutant list 'without taking into account' the health and environmental factors the Clean Water Act normally requires, skipping the case-by-case scientific evaluation those standards usually involve [S3].

The compliance deadline of January 1, 2022 for new discharge and pretreatment standards is aggressive for a large class of thousands of related chemicals, and meeting it could impose significant treatment costs on wastewater systems and their industrial users, some of which would be passed to consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit — controlling a class of persistent chemicals found in drinking water sources — is substantial, and the main costs fall on the industries that discharge PFAS. The genuine design concerns are the statutory shortcut around the usual EPA scientific evaluation and the tight deadlines, which could produce standards shaped more by statute than by agency study. The bill's larger problem is not its design but that it never received any committee action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Water Resources subcommittee the day after introduction, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas introduced the bill on July 2, 2019, with three Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S4][S5].

The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it remained; no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and industrial dischargers are better off because the discharge limits were never set, and the outcome reflects a committee system where most bills introduced without committee leadership support simply die.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial PFAS dischargers; no new limits set

for.name: Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the EPA to regulate PFAS under the Clean Water Act.

for.name: Elissa Slotkin, Brendan Boyle, and Annie Kuster

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Peter DeFazio
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or committee vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: PFAS manufacturers and industrial dischargers
against.role: Industries that produce or discharge PFAS chemicals
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the bill's failure to advance; the chemical industry has broadly opposed new federal PFAS discharge limits.

sides.party_line_note: All four original supporters were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; no Republican ever took action on the bill [S1][S4].

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and users (nonstick products, waterproof textiles, firefighting foam)
industries.note: The bill would have required EPA discharge limits on PFAS, raising treatment and compliance costs for firms that make or use these chemicals. Those costs exist because these persistent chemicals end up in the waterways people rely on.

industries.industry: Industrial water dischargers (paper, metal plating, textiles)
industries.note: Pretreatment standards under Clean Water Act section 307(b) would have required these facilities to remove PFAS before sending wastewater to sewage plants, adding compliance costs.
Pretreatment standards would shift the burden of removing PFAS onto the industrial users upstream, but utilities could also face PFAS limits in their own permits and the cost of upgraded treatment.
